standard_text: Apply the inverse relationship between squaring and finding the square root of a perfect square whole number. Find square roots of perfect square whole numbers.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to find square roots of perfect square whole numbers up to 400 and to apply squaring and square rooting as operations that undo each other, all without a calculator. The on-grade skills move from recognizing perfect squares to finding roots, then run the inverse in both directions: choosing the square root expression that produces a value, and squaring to recover the number under a radical. Students who stall here usually cannot evaluate whole number exponents, misreading 5^2 as 5 x 2, a gap that traces back to grade 6 exponent work. Deeper still, weak multiplication facts and a shaky picture of area leave nothing for squaring to mean. Intervention should rebuild multiplication facts through 12 x 12 in square arrays, reconnect area of a square as side times side, then restore grade 6 skill with powers and order of operations before returning to roots.

steps.rationale: The Below-proficiency demand and the entry point: you must recognize a number as a whole number times itself before you can take its root.
The standard's core verb -- find square roots of perfect square whole numbers -- by recalling which factor was squared, using the harder range up to 400.
The same finding step in a select-the-value format, exposing and correcting the halving and off-by-one errors before the inverse work begins.
The At-proficiency inverse relationship in the value-to-expression direction: to produce k you take the square root of k times k, not k squared.
The inverse relationship in the other direction: undo a square root by squaring to recover the number under it.
The Above-proficiency synthesis (DOK 2): apply squaring and square-rooting as inverse operations that cancel, and justify why.

skills.name: Recall multiplication facts through 12 x 12 using arrays

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply single digit and small two digit factors fluently, seeing each fact as equal rows and columns.

skills.i_do_script: A multiplication fact is a picture: 7 x 7 means 7 rows with 7 dots in each row. Watch: I draw the array and skip count the rows, 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49. So 7 x 7 = 49. When both factors match, the array is a perfect square shape, the same number of rows as columns. I keep the doubles diagonal in my head: 6 x 6 = 36, 7 x 7 = 49, 8 x 8 = 64, up to 12 x 12 = 144. Multiplying is counting equal rows, not adding the two factors.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the factors instead of multiplying them
canonical_error.why: The student treats the times sign like a plus sign. 7 x 7 means 7 rows of 7, which is 49 dots; adding gives only one row plus one column of the story.

skills.name: Find the area of a square or rectangle as rows times columns

prerequisite_skill.description: Find the area of a rectangle or square by multiplying side lengths, understanding area as rows of unit squares.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A square has sides 6 inches long. What is its area?

skills.i_do_script: Area counts the unit squares that cover a shape. Watch: a rectangle 5 units long and 3 units wide is covered by 3 rows of 5 squares, and 3 x 5 = 15, so the area is 15 square units. A square is the special case where the sides match: a square with 6 inch sides is covered by 6 rows of 6 squares, and 6 x 6 = 36 square inches. Area is rows times columns, which is length times width. Adding the sides gives the distance around the shape, not the covering.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the side lengths instead of multiplying, confusing area with perimeter
canonical_error.example: Says the area of a 6 by 4 rectangle is 20 (6 + 4 + 6 + 4) instead of 24
canonical_error.why: The student computes the distance around the shape instead of counting the squares that cover it. Area is rows times columns; the grid picture shows 4 rows of 6 squares, which is 24.

skills.item_template: A square or rectangle with whole number side lengths up to 12. Student finds the area. Short response fluency bank.

skills.name: Evaluate powers with whole number bases and exponents

prerequisite_skill.description: Evaluate whole number expressions with exponents by using the base as a repeated factor.

skills.i_do_script: An exponent counts how many times the base is used as a factor. Watch: 5^2 means 5 x 5 = 25, not 5 x 2. And 2^3 means 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, three factors of 2, not 2 x 3. For a square like 5^2, I can picture a 5 by 5 array: 25 tiles. For 3^4 I multiply step by step: 3 x 3 = 9, 9 x 3 = 27, 27 x 3 = 81. The exponent is a count of factors, never a factor itself.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the base by the exponent instead of using the base as a repeated factor
canonical_error.example: Says 5^2 = 10 (5 x 2) or 4^3 = 12 (4 x 3) instead of 25 and 64
canonical_error.why: The student reads the small raised number as a factor to multiply by. The exponent only counts how many copies of the base to multiply: 4^3 = 4 x 4 x 4 = 64.

skills.item_template: A power with a whole number base (1 to 20) and exponent (2 to 5), kept calculator free. Student evaluates or writes the power. Numeric or multiple choice.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 81 = 3 x 3 x 3 x 3. 12 is base times exponent (3 x 4); 27 is 3^3, one factor short; 64 is 4^3, base and exponent swapped.
4^3 = 4 x 4 x 4 = 64. 4 x 3 = 12 (base times exponent error); 3^4 = 81; 6^2 = 36.

redirect_script.stop: Is the exponent a factor, or a count of factors?
redirect_script.prompt: Write the base out the number of times the exponent says: 4^3 = 4 x 4 x 4. Then multiply left to right: 16, then 64. The exponent never gets multiplied in.
redirect_script.praise: You used the base as a repeated factor, that is what a power means.

skills.name: Use order of operations to evaluate expressions with exponents

prerequisite_skill.description: Evaluate numeric expressions that mix an exponent with other operations, doing parentheses and exponents before multiplying, dividing, adding, or subtracting.

skills.i_do_script: When an exponent sits inside a bigger expression, the exponent gets evaluated before I multiply, divide, add, or subtract. Watch: 2 x 3^2. The exponent belongs only to the 3, so I square first: 3^2 = 9, then multiply: 2 x 9 = 18. If I multiplied first I would get 6^2 = 36, a different problem. Parentheses change the story: (1 + 2)^2 means add first, 3^2 = 9. Exponent before the other operations, unless parentheses say otherwise.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies the exponent to a product or works left to right instead of evaluating the exponent first
canonical_error.example: Computes 2 x 3^2 as (2 x 3)^2 = 36 instead of 2 x 9 = 18
canonical_error.why: The student lets the exponent grab everything to its left. An exponent binds only to the base right under it; the multiplication waits until the power is evaluated.

redirect_script.praise: You evaluated the power first and then finished, that is the right order.

skills.name: Identify which numbers are perfect squares
skills.i_do_script: A perfect square is a whole number that equals some whole number times itself. To test a number, I ask 'is there a whole number that squares to it?' Watch: is 36 a perfect square? Yes -- 6 x 6 = 36. Is 20 a perfect square? No -- 4 x 4 = 16 and 5 x 5 = 25, and 20 sits between them with no whole number in the middle. I check each number against my square facts: 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81 are all perfect squares; numbers like 20 and 75 are not.

canonical_error.pattern: Labels a number a perfect square when it is merely even or close to one
canonical_error.example: Calls 20 a perfect square because it is even and near 16 and 25, though no whole number squares to it
canonical_error.why: The student checks for 'looks squarish' or evenness instead of testing whether a whole number times itself produces it. A perfect square must be exactly n x n for some whole number n.

skills.name: Find the square root of a perfect square whole number
skills.i_do_script: A square root is a side length: if a square holds 196 tiles, the root asks how long each side is. Half of 196 cannot be the side -- a 98-by-98 square would hold nearly ten thousand tiles. To find a square root, I ask 'what whole number, multiplied by itself, gives this number?' Watch the square root of 256. I run through my square facts: 15 x 15 = 225, too small; 16 x 16 = 256 -- that's it. So the square root of 256 is 16. I am NOT dividing by 2; I'm finding the factor that was multiplied by itself. For 144, it's 12, because 12 x 12 = 144.

canonical_error.why: The student treats a square root like 'divide by two' because both shrink the number. A square root asks which whole number times itself gives the value, not what half of it is.

skills.name: Write an expression showing that squaring and square rooting undo each other
skills.i_do_script: You already know squaring and square rooting undo each other. Now you have to write that down as an expression instead of saying it. Watch: I start with 7, square it to get 49, then take the square root of 49 and I am back at 7. Written as one expression that is the square root of 7 squared, and it equals 7. The letter version says the same thing for every number: the square root of n squared equals n. The expression is a sentence, and it says the two operations cancel.

canonical_error.pattern: Writes the two operations side by side rather than nested, so the expression does not actually undo anything
canonical_error.example: Writes 'the square root of n, then n squared' as two separate expressions, or writes n^2 = sqrt(n), treating the inverse relationship as an equality between the two operations
canonical_error.why: The student understands the relationship in words -- one undoes the other -- but has not seen that undoing means applying the second operation TO the result of the first. Nesting is the notation for 'then', and nothing in the spoken version signals it.

strategy_links.why: Think-pair-share on 'why do these operations cancel' builds the DOK-2 justification the standard's top band asks for.
Journaling the general rule ('applying both inverse operations returns the start') consolidates the reasoning.
Studying a correct both-steps example beside a stopped-halfway one targets the single-operation error.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student applies only one operation and doesn't recognize the two cancel.
misconception_redirects.say: Squaring and taking a square root undo each other. Do both: the square root of 25 is 5, then square the 5 to get back 25. Don't stop at the first step.
misconception_redirects.praise: You saw the two operations cancel back to the start -- that's the inverse relationship.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student works the outside operation before the inside one.

misconception_redirects.praise: You applied both operations in order and saw them cancel to the start.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, matching a value to the square root expression that produces it, the At proficiency test of the inverse relationship. If they pass, move up to S5 (undo a square root by squaring to recover the number) and S6 (justify why the two operations cancel). If they fail, drop one grade: B1 checks whether the student can evaluate whole number exponents at all, and B2 checks order of operations when an exponent sits inside a larger expression. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (multiplication facts built in square arrays) and F2 (area as rows times columns) locate the gap in grades 3 and 4. S1, S2, and S3 stay available to probe perfect square recognition and root finding on grade.

pld_descriptors.note: Verbatim from the ILEARN item specification. These are performance bands on THIS standard, not lower-grade content: a student at Below Proficiency is working on this standard at its least complex entry point.
pld_descriptors.below: Identify numbers that are perfect squares. Calculate square roots of perfect square whole numbers less than or equal to 144. Represent the inverse relationship between squaring and square rooting symbolically using numbers or variables in simple expressions.
pld_descriptors.approaching: Calculate square roots of perfect square whole numbers and identify or write equivalent expressions involving square roots and squared numbers using the inverse relationship, including values between 144 and 400. Apply the inverse relationship to determine up to two equivalent expressions for a given whole-number value.
pld_descriptors.at: Find negative square roots of perfect squares. Determine missing values in equality statements involving square roots and squared numbers. Distinguish accurate equivalent expressions from incorrect forms.
pld_descriptors.above: Apply the inverse relationship between squaring and square roots to evaluate, compare, or generate complex expressions involving radicals, exponents, and variables and justify the reasoning used. Analyze statements to determine missing values or verify correctness.
